content: Goosebumps, also referred to as goose pimples, goose flesh, chill bumps, chicken skin, or by the medical term cutis anserina, are small, raised bumps that appear on the skin at the base of body hairs. These bumps develop involuntarily when a person is exposed to cold temperatures or experiences intense emotions such as fear or awe. The physiological reflex responsible for the formation of goosebumps is known as horripilation, piloerection, or the pilomotor reflex. This reflex is not unique to humans and is observed in many other mammals. A notable example is the porcupine, which raises its quills when threatened as a defensive mechanism. Goosebumps are caused by the contraction of tiny muscles located at the base of each hair follicle, known as arrectores pilorum. When these muscles contract, they pull the hair upright, creating the characteristic bumps on the skin. This reflex is initiated by the sympathetic nervous system, which is also responsible for other fight-or-flight responses. In response to cold, the erect hairs in animals with fur or dense hair trap a layer of air close to the skin, providing insulation and helping to retain body heat. In situations of anger or fear, the erect hairs can make an animal appear larger and more intimidating to potential threats. This phenomenon can be observed in the intimidation displays of chimpanzees, stressed mice and rats, and frightened cats. In humans, goosebumps can also occur as a reaction to auditory stimuli, such as the sound of nails scratching on a chalkboard, or to emotionally powerful experiences, such as listening to awe-inspiring music. However, in humans, piloerection as a response to cold or fear is considered vestigial, as humans have relatively little body hair, and the reflex no longer serves a functional purpose. Goosebumps are most commonly observed on the forearms in humans but can also appear on the legs, back, and other areas of the skin with hair. In some individuals, they may even occur on the face or scalp. Rarely, piloerection can be a symptom of certain medical conditions, such as temporal lobe epilepsy, some brain tumors, or autonomic hyperreflexia. Goosebumps can also be triggered during heroin withdrawal. A skin condition known as keratosis pilaris can mimic the appearance of goosebumps, though it is unrelated to the pilomotor reflex. Goosebumps occur exclusively in mammals, as other animals lack hair. The term goosebumps is somewhat misleading, as the bumps on the skin of a plucked goose are not caused by piloerection, even though the term originates from this visual similarity. Birds, however, do have a similar reflex in which they raise their feathers to retain warmth. The Latin root horrere, meaning to tremble, is the origin of words such as horrific and horror. In other languages, the term for goosebumps often substitutes goose with other types of poultry. For example, in French, it is referred to as la chair de poule (hen's flesh), in Dutch as kippenvel (chicken skin), in Spanish as la carne de gallina (hen's flesh), and in Chinese as 雞皮疙瘩 (chicken skin bumps).
